newsitem.title: UK: Britain's utilities take windfall tax in stride.
newsitem.headline: Britain's utilities take windfall tax in stride.

text.p: British water and electricity stocks showed strong gains on Thursday as the market breathed a sigh of relief that a one-off tax on excess profits announced by Chancellor Gordon Brown in his first budget on Wednesday was close to expectations, analysts said.

But multi-utility Hyder Plc bucked the trend, as its shares closed down 13.5 pence at 810 pence after touching a low of 772 pence, weighed by worries that its 280 million pound ($469.3 million) share of the total 5.2 billion pound levy would mean it had to raise funds.
"Although the uncertainty risk has left most prices, some think Hyder may have to issue some paper to pay for this," said Geraint Anderson, utilities analyst at SocGen.
Brown said the tax should raise around 2.1 billion pounds from the electricity sector, some 1.65 billion from water companies and another 1.45 billion from other privatised utilities.

The tax will be charged at a rate of 23 percent on the difference between company value at the time of flotation and company value calculated by reference to net profits over a period up to four years following privatisation.

"The formula was clearly aimed at hitting water companies hardest, they paid low taxes and have therefore been exposed by the emphasis on post-tax profits," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
But relief that the tax was close to expectations of around five billion pounds gave a boost to most shares of water and electricity companies.
Anglian Water, which said it would have to pay 170 million, saw its shares gain 14 pence to close at 723 pence while Thames Water, set to pay 230 million, jumped 26 pence to 766 pence.

In the electricity sector, shares in Southern Electric, which faces a bill for 165 million, closed at 460 pence, up 23.5 pence, while generator National Power, which estimated it would pay 261 million, shot up 35.5 pence to 569.5 pence.
"The risk of the windfall tax is now quantified, it's a one-off and the cost will be split over two years, which is beneficial to cash flow," Anderson said.

The new Labour government has targeted a windfall tax on privatised utilities well before it swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, although details of total revenue and formulae for calculating the levy were not divulged until Wednesday.
Water and electricity stocks have been largely discounting a levy of around five billion for some time and analysts said Thursday's gains were bringing prices back up to normal valuation levels.
"These stocks had been on a very big risk premium, now that's unwinding and you're seeing some substantial gains," the analyst said.

In addition, there are hopes that companies will now return to providing benefits to shareholders in the form of buybacks and strong dividends, as they adjust to the real impact of the tax, analysts said.
"I think a lot of companies will do buybacks over the next year now the windfall tax is known, such as Anglian Water, Severn Trent, South West Water, Thames, Wessex and Yorkshire Water," he said.

Severn Trent indicated some of the confidence companies were feeling when it announced on Monday, two days before the budget, that it would complete a 10 percent buyback of shares having bought 5.6 percent in December.
Some companies warned that they would have to borrow to fund the tax take, including Anglian Water and U.S.-owned Midlands Electricity.

Hyder said it would review the effect of the tax on its future plans and would make a further statement in due course, but the market worried that its high gearing of some 156 percent would mean it would have to borrow and that its dividend growth might be hit.
"Hyder is the major loser out of it all, that's why it's bucking the market," said the analyst.
($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
